stances.claim: CJ did NOT equate the Sereno removal with the two unidentified erring justices or the Arroyo/Enrile/Estrada decisions -- he cited Sereno 'only because they exemplify how our Supreme Court disciplines its own members, while the Supreme Court of the United States (Scotus) has yet to do so.'

CJ restates his prior position: the 8-6 decision ousting Sereno was (1) 'plainly unconstitutional' because -- IMHO -- SC justices may be removed 'only via impeachment expressly canalized by our Constitution and only for the grounds provided therein, not via quo warranto'; (2) 'unduly harsh' because expressly made immediately executory, so 'the embarrassed and belittled erstwhile chief justice had to leave the Supreme Court premises carrying all her personal belongings' the very day. 'Decisions convicting even the most hardened criminals are not immediately executory. They could still file motions for reconsideration that would stay immediate execution.'

Rule-of-law discipline: 'Though I disagreed with the decision, I must follow it and cite it as a valid judgment.' Same for any decision (including Arroyo/Enrile/Estrada): 'I must respect and obey them. That is the rule of law. As I always say, we can disagree without being disagreeable and we can differ without being difficult.'

Justices must render full-time service and shed political/business/professional connections -- 'No side incomes.' CJ's own example: he 'dissolved my law firm when I ascended to the Court in 1995 to heed the Constitution's call for proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.' Dissolution was not required (only resignation), but CJ thought it best to adhere to the Court's ideal of being 'like Caesar's wife, beyond suspicion.'

The Gesmundo Court has not been tested by 'nation-shaking cases comparable to those of the Concepcion Court on the ratification of the 1973 Constitution, or of the Davide Court on stopping the House of Representatives from impeaching the chief justice, or of the Panganiban Court on rejecting the people's initiative to change our presidential system to the parliamentary' -- but CJ is 'still impressed by its solid effort to implement the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027.'

Personal transition: prior June 3 and 10 columns covered three talented grandkids' master's-degree scholarships from top US universities 'without their applying.' Now 'a fourth apo,' Katrina P. Hannett, was offered bioethics-master's scholarships by Johns Hopkins, NYU, and Penn.

Katrina biography: gifted; in kindergarten taught a fellow 5-year-old cursive script; in first grade given fourth-grade-level work; 'did her homework lying upside down on a sofa, feet up on a wall, and hair cascading down the chair to the floor'; still got top grades; 'elected student body president (like her Lolo).' Compassion-and-humility traits: first to hug crying offender (sibling who pushed her); eighth-grade prima-donna dancer who pulled back to avoid 'dramas' among beat dancers; medical volunteer at marathons saving cardiac-arrest victims. Aspires to be 'a compassionate doctor'; pre-med master's in bioethics. 'She will crack her mega-class dilemma soon.'

one_paragraph_summary: CJ is 'totally amazed' at the emails, calls, and texts on his prior June 17 column 'From awe to dismay at the Scotus' -- samples: 'Disgusting, the Scotus is no longer the highest court we admire'; 'No different from politicians'; 'I hope Amb. MaryKay Carlson reported this to her superiors to stop the self-destruct of the Scotus.' It even rated a full column from Manila Overseas Press Club prexy Tony Lopez ('The decline of Scotus,' Philippine Star, 6/18/24). Two reader questions need response: (1) Why equate CJ Sereno's removal with the two unidentified erring justices? (2) Did you forget the dismaying decisions involving Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Juan Ponce Enrile, and Jinggoy Estrada? CJ clarifies: he did NOT equate those three decisions -- he cited Sereno only because they 'exemplify how our Supreme Court disciplines its own members, while the Supreme Court of the United States (Scotus) has yet to do so.' He restates his prior position: the 8-6 decision ousting Sereno was (1) 'plainly unconstitutional' because -- IMHO -- Supreme Court justices may be removed 'only via impeachment expressly canalized by our Constitution and only for the grounds provided therein, not via quo warranto'; and (2) 'unduly harsh' because expressly made immediately executory -- 'on the very day it was issued, the embarrassed and belittled erstwhile chief justice had to leave the Supreme Court premises carrying all her personal belongings. Decisions convicting even the most hardened criminals are not immediately executory. They could still file motions for reconsideration that would stay immediate execution.' Rule-of-law discipline: 'Though I disagreed with the decision, I must follow it and cite it as a valid judgment.' Same for the Arroyo/Enrile/Estrada decisions: 'I must respect and obey them. That is the rule of law. As I always say, we can disagree without being disagreeable and we can differ without being difficult.' Justices must render full-time service and shed political, business, and professional connections -- 'No side incomes.' CJ's own example: he 'dissolved my law firm when I ascended to the Court in 1995 to heed the Constitution's call for proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence' -- dissolution was not legally required (only resignation), but he chose to adhere to the ideal of being 'like Caesar's wife, beyond suspicion.' The Gesmundo Court has not been tested by 'nation-shaking cases comparable to those of the Concepcion Court on the ratification of the 1973 Constitution, or of the Davide Court on stopping the House of Representatives from impeaching the chief justice, or of the Panganiban Court on rejecting the people's initiative to change our presidential system to the parliamentary' -- but CJ is 'still impressed by its solid effort to implement the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027.' Then the personal transition: amazing comments also came on his June 3 and 10 columns about master's-degree scholarships granted to his three talented grandkids by top US universities 'without their applying.' This proud Lolo just learned that a fourth 'apo,' Katrina P. Hannett, was offered bioethics-master's scholarships. CJ recounts: Katrina was gifted from kindergarten -- taught a fellow 5-year-old cursive script when he didn't yet write in print; in first grade she was given fourth-grade-level work to keep her busy; 'She did her homework lying upside down on a sofa, feet up on a wall, and hair cascading down the chair to the floor. Still, she got top grades and was elected student body president (like her Lolo).' Her compassion-and-humility traits stand out: when her sibling was scolded for pushing her around, she was 'the first to hug her crying offender'; as an eighth-grade dancer landing prima donna roles, she pulled back to avoid 'dramas' among beat dancers; now as a young adult she does medical-volunteer marathon work helping save cardiac-arrest runners. She aspires to be a 'compassionate doctor' and chose a pre-med master's in bioethics -- 'the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in medicine.' Scholarships offered by Johns Hopkins, NYU, and Penn. She hasn't made her final choice -- 'maybe still pondering real-world human issues?' -- but 'she will crack her mega-class dilemma soon.'
